grammar.title: Grammatik
grammar.rule: wir sind · ihr seid · sie sind · wir tragen · ihr tragt · sie tragen
grammar.note_en:
Plural means more than one. The subject pronoun wir means “we”: the speaker belongs to the group. Ihr means “you” when addressing several people informally; singular du still addresses one person. Sie now also means “they,” referring to a group already identified. Compare Wir sind hier (“We are here”), Ihr seid hier (“You [plural] are here”), and Sie tragen den Tisch (“They carry the table”). The last sentence refers to Ben and Nora together. Singular sie meaning “she” remains available: the finite verb and context distinguish Sie trägt (“She carries”) from Sie tragen (“They carry”). This chapter does not introduce formal Sie.

With wir and plural sie, present verbs normally end in -en, matching their dictionary form: wir wohnen / sie wohnen (“we live / they live”), wir arbeiten / sie arbeiten (“we work / they work”). With ihr, most end in -t: ihr habt (“you have”), ihr helft (“you help”), ihr tragt (“you carry”). Arbeiten needs its extra e: ihr arbeitet (“you work”), just as du arbeitest did. Singular er/sie/es arbeitet and plural ihr arbeitet have the same printed form but different subjects. Sein is irregular: wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind (“we are, you are, they are”). The table includes forms for comparison, but drills require only forms already demonstrated in the story. Helfen is used without an object here; its object construction comes with later case teaching.

A noun's plural form must be learned with the noun. Do not add -s to every German noun. Tisch → Tische (“table → tables”) adds -e. Stuhl → Stühle (“chair → chairs”) adds both an umlaut and -e. Frau → Frauen (“woman → women”) adds -en; Nachbar → Nachbarn (“neighbour → neighbours”) adds -n. Leute means “people” and is plural in this use. The definite article for every noun gender in nominative or accusative plural is die: Die Tische stehen hier (“The tables stand here”), Wir nehmen die Stühle (“We take the chairs”). There is no plural indefinite article ein. Use a bare plural or a number: zwei Stühle (“two chairs”), drei Leute (“three people”), vier Leute (“four people”), fünf Leute (“five people”). No dative plural is taught here.

Adjectives after ist or sind keep the same form: Der Tisch ist alt (“The table is old”), Der Tisch ist neu (“The table is new”). The predicate adjectives alt and neu (“old” and “new”) do not change for gender or number. Neu can mean new or newly arrived: Mira ist neu hier (“Mira is new here”). Zusammen means “together,” while alle refers to the whole identified group: Alle helfen (“Everyone helps”). It takes a plural verb in this sentence. Ben and Nora live in the same house, making them Nachbarn (“neighbours”); Freund and Freundin identify male and female friends. The story brings people together to solve the furniture problem and then changes its question through the photograph. The people shown there belong to the earlier courtyard scene; the present narrative does not identify either woman yet.

Tragen (“carry”) changes its stem in singular sie trägt (“she carries”), but not in wir tragen (“we carry”) or ihr tragt (“you [plural] carry”). Helfen (“help”) similarly gives ich helfe (“I help”), du hilfst (“you [singular] help”), sie hilft (“she helps”), wir helfen (“we help”) and ihr helft (“you [plural] help”). The plural stems return to a, e respectively; do not copy the singular umlaut or i into them.
